title: When Skills Remain but Access Fails:Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization

paper.title: When Skills Remain but Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
paper.abstract: Abstract Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization. Using correct-skill-address reactivation as a diagnostic, we identify a hierarchical pattern: closed-book execution can collapse while supplying the correct skill address substantially restores learned behavior, and continued optimization later degrades execution even under the correct skill address. We call these two regimes skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting . Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM) , which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory . At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% shard-routing accuracy across two task orders, improving over Progressive-LoRA by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples. These results support an Address–Execution view of continual skill retention, in which stable procedural content and reliable access are distinct design problems.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable Skills to organize tool use, environment interaction, and multi-step action generation ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . A Skill packages procedural guidance into a workflow: which operations to invoke, how their inputs are constructed, and how intermediate steps depend on one another ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Most skill-based systems still keep this guidance outside the model and retrieve the relevant Skill text at inference time. Execution therefore depends both on retrieval and on the model’s ability to follow the retrieved description. Long contexts are used unevenly, irrelevant context can distract reasoning, and detailed Skill documentation may not reliably improve execution ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2023 ; Li and others, 2026 ) . Recent work on Skill Internalization moves this procedural guidance into model parameters, allowing learned behavior to be used without repeatedly injecting the Skill description ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Zhang and Qi, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . We consider agents that acquire new Skills over time. In this continual-learning setting, disjoint Skill families arrive sequentially, the model internalizes these Skills in sequence, and the final model receives only the user request at inference time, without a Skill family label, Skill name, or retrieved Skill card, while retaining the capabilities of all earlier Skills ( Parisi et al., 2019 ; De Lange et al., 2022 ; van de Ven and Tolias, 2019 ) . Existing skill-internalization studies do not establish whether earlier Skills remain usable after later Skills are learned. During continual Skill Internalization training, old-Skill closed-book performance can fall to zero within only a few optimization steps after training moves to a new Skill family. Successful internalization does not by itself ensure retention. The collapse in closed-book performance hides a more structured failure. At a checkpoint that fails all 408 old-task requests, supplying the correct skill address , given by the benchmark’s exact procedure identifier or identifiers required by the request, restores execution performance from 0 to 69.85%. Because this address also reveals the target node identity, we use it as a diagnostic rather than an information-neutral access probe. With further optimization, execution under the correct skill address degrades, and the same ordering appears across SFT, GRPO, and SKILL0. We call the two regimes skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting: closed-book execution fails first while execution under the correct skill address remains recoverable, before that recoverability itself erodes. Figure 1: Continual skill internalization and hierarchical forgetting. (a) Sequential learning can erase old-task closed-book performance within a few optimization steps. (b) A matched request-level example exposes two stages of forgetting. During addressing forgetting, the correct Skill name recovers execution that the raw request no longer reaches. Continued optimization can later damage execution under the correct skill address itself. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM) , which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory . The reactivation diagnostic exposes the Address–Execution split at individual-skill granularity; FSM operationalizes the same split more coarsely, using stage-level shards that each contain multiple Skills. At each stage, FSM trains and freezes one new LoRA executor while Address Memory learns request-to-shard associations without retaining historical requests or execution trajectories. The selected executor still identifies and composes the required Skills within its shard. At inference, Address Memory selects one shard from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a language-model generation. We make three contributions: • We construct a five-stage benchmark for continual skill internalization by partitioning 100 TaskBench Skills into disjoint Skill families and evaluating sequential acquisition, retention, and autonomous closed-book access. • We identify a hierarchical forgetting pattern under canonical-name reactivation: closed-book execution can collapse while execution under the correct skill address remains recoverable, before that recoverability also erodes. • We introduce FSM , which separates plastic Address Memory from frozen Execution Memory. Across two task orders, FSM reaches 65.95% mean performance and 93.38% shard-routing accuracy, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay.

sections.heading: Skill Internalization.
sections.text: Agent Skills are commonly represented as procedural artifacts that are retrieved and inserted into the model context at inference time ( Li and others, 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Recent work studies how to convert this guidance into persistent model behavior. SKILL0 and SkillC learn to execute Skills with progressively less dependence on explicit Skill context ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Another line of work parameterizes procedural knowledge directly: Skill-to-LoRA and ParametricSkills map Skills into adapter parameters, while LatentSkill and PEAM move textual or experiential Skill information into in-weight representations ( Zhang and Qi, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . LifeSkill further studies online lifelong adaptation from Skill-guided experience ( Mao et al., 2026 ) . Together, these methods show that procedural guidance can be transferred from context into model parameters, and several introduce mechanisms for accumulating such capabilities over time. Our focus is the failure structure that emerges when internalized Skills are learned sequentially without Skill identity at test time. We distinguish loss of request-side access from loss of execution itself, and use this Address–Execution hierarchy to determine what should remain plastic and what should be protected during continual internalization.

sections.heading: Continual Learning.
sections.text: Continual learning studies how models acquire new tasks without overwriting earlier competence. Replay preserves old examples, regularization constrains parameter changes, and architectural methods isolate or expand parameters for new tasks ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Li and Hoiem, 2018 ; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017 ; Rebuffi et al., 2017b ; Rusu et al., 2016 ) . The last family is especially relevant when different tasks require distinct behaviors. Adapter-based continual learning allocates task-specific parameters ( Madotto et al., 2021 ) ; EPI combines private parameter-efficient modules with a non-parametric task identifier so that the appropriate module can be recovered without storing old training data ( Wang et al., 2023c ) ; and MoCL continually adds and composes modules to preserve knowledge while supporting transfer ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . FSM falls within this modular parameter-isolation line, with its decomposition motivated by the failure structure of continual Skill internalization. In continual Skill internalization, our reactivation experiments show that request-to-Skill access can fail while conditional execution remains intact. FSM therefore isolates the acquired procedural execution in frozen multi-Skill shards and treats access as the updated memory state.

sections.heading: Problem setting.
sections.text: We consider a sequence of stages t = 1 , … , T t=1,\ldots,T , where each stage introduces a previously unseen skill set 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and corresponding request–workflow supervision. The skill sets are pairwise disjoint, and after stage t t the desired competence includes all skills in 𝒮 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mathcal{S}_{t} . For a request x x , successful closed-book execution requires the model to produce the correct request-conditioned workflow using only the raw request. Training may use stage-local workflow supervision and, for skill-guided baselines, textual skill cards. Evaluation is autonomous and closed-book: the model receives only x x , not a stage label, skill name, or catalog. This setting tests acquisition of new skills and retention of earlier skills under autonomous inference. Benchmark. We instantiate this stream using the public Microsoft TaskBench benchmark ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , partitioning its 100 canonical skills into five disjoint semantic families (Table 3 ). We use each family as a unit of continual acquisition: a capability package containing several related procedures. The five packages contain 40, 11, 21, 9, and 19 canonical skills. Requests can require multi-node workflows composed from several skills in the same package. Each stage contains 1,000 training requests, for 5,000 in total, and the five held-out sets contain 2,186 requests. The complete skill inventory and output contract appear in Appendix A . sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Our primary metric is exact-match task success (EM) , which requires the complete prescribed workflow output to be correct; for TaskBench this is the benchmark’s canonical graph exact match, but we refer to it simply as EM in the main text. The T1–T5 columns and their task-macro average all report this same quantity. We use three secondary diagnostics to interpret failures: Tool-choice accuracy checks whether the ordered tool sequence is correct while ignoring request-specific values; Argument-value F1 compares predicted and target ( skill , argument , value ) (\text{skill},\text{argument},\text{value}) tuples; and BWT measures final old-task EM minus EM immediately after that task was learned, with zero indicating no forgetting; additional benchmark-specific metrics appear in the appendix.

sections.heading: Direct continual optimization rapidly eliminates old-task closed-book performance.
sections.text: Before introducing any mechanism for preservation, we first measure how direct continual optimization behaves when training moves away from an acquired task. Immediately after learning the old task, EM is 77.45% for SFT, 84.31% for GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and 84.07% for the SKILL0 ( Lu et al., 2026 ) curriculum. After optimization switches to the next task, old-task EM falls to zero at observed steps 8, 6, and 10, respectively, and remains there over the rest of the measured interval (Figure 2 ). Across hundreds of held-out requests, none of the old-task outputs remain exactly correct. Under the standard closed-book criterion, all three procedures therefore exhibit catastrophic forgetting of the previously internalized skill. This endpoint shows that retention has failed without revealing which part of the acquired capability was lost. Section 4 tests this distinction directly.

sections.heading: 4.1 Correct-Skill-Address Reactivation
sections.text: Section 3 showed that old-task closed-book performance can fall to zero after continual optimization moves to a new task. That endpoint does not reveal whether the old procedure has been erased or whether the model has lost access to behavior that is still present. We distinguish these cases with a controlled reactivation intervention. We take a post-forgetting checkpoint that scores zero on all 408 closed-book T2 requests and supply only the correct skill address , given by the benchmark’s exact procedure identifier or identifiers required by each request. On the same frozen model, full-task EM recovers from 0 to 69.85%. The address provides no argument values, workflow steps, or target serialization, so the model must still construct the request-conditioned workflow. Because it also reveals the gold node identity, we use the correct skill address as a diagnostic rather than a pure access probe. Additional controls are reported in Appendix B.1 . A frozen-base control further separates address recognition from learned execution. On 408 T2 requests, frozen Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) selects the correct skill on 92.65% of examples when given the correct skill address but obtains 0% full-task EM; by contrast, the post-forgetting checkpoint recovers 69.85% under the same address after request-only performance reaches zero. Recognizing the supplied address alone therefore cannot account for the recovered behavior. We use Address for access to the relevant procedural state and Execution for producing the request-conditioned workflow once that state is available. This reversal shows that substantial execution remains available once the correct procedure identity is supplied; we call this regime skill-addressing forgetting .

sections.heading: 4.2 Execution under the correct skill address erodes later
sections.text: Figure 2: Hierarchical forgetting during continual skill internalization. Top: during the T2 → \rightarrow T3 transition, closed-book Task2 EM can collapse while Task2 remains recoverable when the correct skill address is supplied; with continued optimization, execution under the correct skill address can also erode. The frozen-executor diagnostic preserves the old task while learning Task3. Bottom: five-stage evaluation matrices for four continual-learning conditions. Off-diagonal cells report closed-book / + Correct Skill Address EM. Across both rows, pale green denotes retained performance, pale yellow denotes addressing forgetting, and pale purple denotes execution forgetting. Diagonal cells show task-acquisition EM. The FSM column is our method. To see what happens after this access failure, Figure 2 follows the first 20 optimizer steps of the T2 → \rightarrow T3 transition, evaluating each checkpoint closed-book and with the correct skill address. When closed-book T2 first reaches zero, full-task EM under the correct skill address is still 76.96% for SFT, 84.07% for GRPO, and 77.70% for SKILL0. Because the paired measurements come from the same checkpoint, this gap shows a loss of autonomous closed-book access relative to the target-identity-assisted condition while conditional execution remains available. Further T3 optimization then reduces performance under the correct skill address from 77.45% to 58.82% for SFT, from 84.56% to 57.60% for GRPO, and from 85.29% to zero for SKILL0. We call this later failure skill-execution forgetting : even the correct address can no longer recover the earlier behavior. The bottom matrices show the same ordering across other continual-learning methods: closed-book performance can collapse before execution under the correct skill address. This diagnostic operates at individual-skill granularity. FSM applies the same functional separation at shard granularity: routing selects a multi-skill capability package, while the selected executor still performs within-shard skill selection, composition, and execution.

sections.heading: 5 Factorized Skill Memory
sections.text: Section 4 separates request-side access from execution at individual-skill granularity. FSM preserves this functional split without allocating one executor per skill: related skills are grouped into stage-level execution shards, and Address Memory learns only which shard to read. Formally, ℳ t = ( A t , ℰ t ) , \mathcal{M}_{t}=(A_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t}), where A t A_{t} is Address Memory and ℰ t = { E 1 , … , E t } \mathcal{E}_{t}=\{E_{1},\ldots,E_{t}\} is Execution Memory . Address remains plastic as new skill families arrive, whereas Execution Memory is append-only. At stage t t , FSM trains and freezes a fresh executor E t E_{t} on 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} ; current requests update Address with shard identity t t and are then discarded. Historical requests and workflow trajectories are never replayed. Each shard contains 9–40 canonical skills, so shard routing only narrows the execution space to a capability package. It does not replace within-shard skill selection: the chosen executor must still recover the required skill sequence, request-specific arguments, and dependencies from the raw request. At inference, Address selects one shard and only that executor performs language-model generation. Figure 3 summarizes the write-and-read process; Appendix A provides further details. sections.heading: 5.1 Execution Memory: Immutable Parametric Shards
sections.text: Let B B denote the shared frozen base model. At stage t t , FSM initializes a fresh LoRA executor E t = B ⊕ Δ t E_{t}=B\oplus\Delta_{t} , trains Δ t \Delta_{t} only on current-stage skill-execution supervision, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to the bank, ℰ t = ℰ t − 1 ∪ { E t } \mathcal{E}_{t}=\mathcal{E}_{t-1}\cup\{E_{t}\} . No subsequent stage updates an earlier Δ j \Delta_{j} . This boundary follows the failure pattern in Section 4 : conditional execution can survive after request-side access has failed, so FSM protects the parameters that store execution and places subsequent adaptation in Address Memory. Low-rank adapters provide a compact implementation of these isolated parametric writes ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Rebuffi et al., 2017a ; Houlsby et al., 2019 ) . Each shard stores a family of related skills rather than a single procedure. For example, the T1 shard contains 40 canonical skills; selecting T1 only determines which execution memory to read, while the executor still chooses and composes the required skills and produces the complete request-conditioned graph. The shared 8.2B backbone is stored once. Under our rank-16 LoRA configuration on the q / k / v / o q/k/v/o projections, each Qwen3-8B shard adds 15.34M parameters, about 0.19% of the backbone, and the complete five-shard bank adds 76.68M parameters, about 0.94%. The five BF16 LoRA deltas occupy about 146 MiB, and inference activates only the selected LoRA.

sections.heading: 5.2 Address Memory: Continual Associative Indexing
sections.text: With earlier execution shards fixed, the continually updated state is the request-to-shard index p Address ​ ( j ∣ x ) , j ∈ { 1 , … , t } . p_{\mathrm{Address}}(j\mid x),\qquad j\in\{1,\ldots,t\}. The test request contains no task label, correct skill address, or skill catalog, so shard identity must be recovered from request text alone. Our deployed Address maps request text into a fixed-dimensional hashing representation and updates an incremental Naive Bayes classifier using only the current request pool with label t t . After the update, those requests are discarded; the retained state consists only of class and feature statistics. Address Memory can therefore absorb new request-to-shard associations without retaining historical requests while the executor bank stays fixed.

sections.heading: 5.3 Single-Shard Memory Read
sections.text: At inference, FSM performs a hard memory read: j ⋆ = arg ⁡ max j ​ p Address ​ ( j ∣ x ) , y = E j ⋆ ​ ( x ) . j^{\star}=\arg\max_{j}p_{\mathrm{Address}}(j\mid x),\qquad y=E_{j^{\star}}(x). The read is single-shard but multi-skill: Address selects one capability package, and the chosen executor can compose several canonical skills from that package while resolving request-specific arguments and graph dependencies. The language-model cost is one executor generation per request. Because Address uses hashing plus Naive Bayes, shard selection requires neither an additional language-model forward pass nor bank-wide scoring.

sections.heading: 6.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We evaluate whether continually internalized skills remain usable after later skill families are acquired. Our primary experiments use Qwen3-8B with rank-16 LoRA on the q / k / v / o q/k/v/o projections; Qwen3-4B provides an additional model-scale robustness check. Each stage executor is trained for six epochs with learning rate 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} and effective batch size eight, then frozen permanently. Evaluation uses greedy decoding with thinking disabled and a 768-token generation cap. We report both task orders from Section 3 . At test time, FSM receives only the raw request: its replay-free Address Memory selects one stage-level execution shard, and only that frozen executor generates the workflow.

Oracle itself still lies 28.24 points below perfect EM after the correct shard is supplied, because the selected executor must recover the skill sequence, arguments, dependencies, and complete workflow. Thus both access and within-shard execution contribute materially to the final error. The task-level pattern makes this split concrete. T2 is mostly access-limited: Oracle reaches 83.58% / 83.33%, FSM 78.19% in both orders, and Self-route 58.82% / 56.62%. T1 is mostly execution-limited because FSM nearly matches an Oracle that reaches only 45.02% / 45.49%. T3 is mixed: Oracle remains above 73%, while all learned selectors leave a larger gap; AdapterCL is stronger than FSM on this family. T4 again lies close to Oracle, whereas Self-route slightly exceeds FSM on T5. These differences show why a single final EM score is insufficient: some families are dominated by access error and others by the execution quality of the selected shard. FSM’s macro advantage comes mainly from recovering the access-sensitive cases while remaining competitive elsewhere. With the execution bank fixed, offline Address reaches 69.15% mean EM and 97.03% routing accuracy, versus 65.95% and 93.38% for sequential Address (Appendix B.5 ). This 3.20-point difference serves as a historical-request reference rather than an isolated replay effect, because the two selectors also differ in both representation and classifier family (hashing+NB versus TF–IDF+LR). The stronger offline selector closes a noticeable portion of the remaining Oracle gap, indicating that improved request-to-shard access still offers meaningful headroom beyond the deployed sequential Address. FSM avoids bank-wide language-model scoring: Address performs a lightweight request-to-shard lookup, activates one frozen LoRA, and uses only one executor generation for each incoming request. Each rank-16 execution shard adds 15.34M parameters; five shards add 76.68M, or only 0.94% of the shared 8.2B backbone. The backbone itself is stored only once, and only the selected LoRA is activated during inference. As Execution Memory grows, storage therefore increases with the number of frozen shards, while the per-request language-model cost remains a single executor generation.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Correct-skill-address reactivation reveals a hierarchical forgetting pattern: closed-book execution can collapse while execution under the correct skill address remains substantially recoverable, and continued optimization can later erase that recoverability as well. FSM follows this distinction by keeping Address Memory plastic and storing acquired procedures in frozen, multi-skill Execution Memory shards that remain unchanged during later stages. Across two five-stage task orders, FSM reaches 65.9593.38percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay. These results support a simple design principle for continual skill memory: preserve acquired procedural content while allowing access to adapt as the skill stream grows. They also separate two remaining sources of error: Address determines which execution shard is reached, whereas the selected shard determines how well the requested workflow is executed. This decomposition makes retention failures more interpretable and suggests where additional capacity or supervision is most useful.

sections.text: This appendix records the benchmark protocol, evaluation contract, metrics, FSM implementation, information budgets, and safeguards used for the main results.

sections.heading: A.1 Continual internalization protocol
sections.text: At stage t t , the learner receives request–graph pairs from a previously unseen skill set 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and then moves to 𝒮 t + 1 \mathcal{S}_{t+1} . The skill sets are pairwise disjoint, and earlier skills remain part of the target competence. For a request x x , the model must produce an executable graph g g : nodes specify canonical skills and arguments, and directed edges encode producer–consumer dependencies. Training may use graph supervision and, for skill-guided baselines, textual skill cards. Evaluation is closed-book: the model receives only x x , with no stage label, skill name, catalog, demonstration, retrieved memory, or target graph. We evaluate two complete task orders, O ​ 1 = [ T ​ 1 , T ​ 2 , T ​ 3 , T ​ 4 , T ​ 5 ] O1=[T1,T2,T3,T4,T5] and O ​ 2 = [ T ​ 3 , T ​ 1 , T ​ 5 , T ​ 2 , T ​ 4 ] O2=[T3,T1,T5,T2,T4] . The primary metric is exact match of the canonical skill graph. Component metrics separate errors in skill selection, argument values, and dependency edges. Backward transfer measures how performance on earlier tasks changes after later stages. All reported aggregates are task macros, so each family has equal weight despite different held-out set sizes.

sections.heading: A.6 Information budgets and comparator roles
sections.text: The selectors differ in the information they receive. Oracle uses the source family label to measure conditional execution. Self-route sees executor generations and token scores but no family label. FSM receives the current request pool during training, retains only classifier statistics, and runs one selected executor at test time. FSM-Offline revisits the full historical request set. Replay uses old request–workflow pairs during training. These budgets define the comparisons: Oracle–FSM includes residual addressing and executor error. FSM-Offline–FSM is a historical-request reference rather than an isolated replay ablation, because the two Address variants also use different feature representations and classifiers.

Separate result summaries track learned Address, Sequential Address, semantic controls, and template-group controls. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.15492v1 [cs.AI] 11 Oct 2026 When Skills Remain but Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization Haomiao Qiu Yining Tang Hongyi Wan Changfeng Sun Ziyue Qiao Miao Zhang Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen Affiliation: Great Bay University Affiliation: Zhejiang University Email: 8.31024B951058@stu.hit.edu.cn Abstract Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization. Using correct-skill-address reactivation as a diagnostic, we identify a hierarchical pattern: closed-book execution can collapse while supplying the correct skill address substantially restores learned behavior, and continued optimization later degrades execution even under the correct skill address. We call these two regimes skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting . Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM) , which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory . At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% shard-routing accuracy across two task orders, improving over Progressive-LoRA by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples. These results support an Address–Execution view of continual skill retention, in which stable procedural content and reliable access are distinct design problems. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution; † Co-corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable Skills to organize tool use, environment interaction, and multi-step action generation ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) . A Skill packages procedural guidance into a workflow: which operations to invoke, how their inputs are constructed, and how intermediate steps depend on one another ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Most skill-based systems still keep this guidance outside the model and retrieve the relevant Skill text at inference time. Execution therefore depends both on retrieval and on the model’s ability to follow the retrieved description. Long contexts are used unevenly, irrelevant context can distract reasoning, and detailed Skill documentation may not reliably improve execution ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2023 ; Li and others, 2026 ) . Recent work on Skill Internalization moves this procedural guidance into model parameters, allowing learned behavior to be used without repeatedly injecting the Skill description ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Zhang and Qi, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . We consider agents that acquire new Skills over time. In this continual-learning setting, disjoint Skill families arrive sequentially, the model internalizes these Skills in sequence, and the final model receives only the user request at inference time, without a Skill family label, Skill name, or retrieved Skill card, while retaining the capabilities of all earlier Skills ( Parisi et al., 2019 ; De Lange et al., 2022 ; van de Ven and Tolias, 2019 ) . Existing skill-internalization studies do not establish whether earlier Skills remain usable after later Skills are learned. During continual Skill Internalization training, old-Skill closed-book performance can fall to zero within only a few optimization steps after training moves to a new Skill family. Successful internalization does not by itself ensure retention. The collapse in closed-book performance hides a more structured failure. At a checkpoint that fails all 408 old-task requests, supplying the correct skill address , given by the benchmark’s exact procedure identifier or identifiers required by the request, restores execution performance from 0 to 69.85%. Because this address also reveals the target node identity, we use it as a diagnostic rather than an information-neutral access probe. With further optimization, execution under the correct skill address degrades, and the same ordering appears across SFT, GRPO, and SKILL0. We call the two regimes skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting: closed-book execution fails first while execution under the correct skill address remains recoverable, before that recoverability itself erodes. Figure 1: Continual skill internalization and hierarchical forgetting. (a) Sequential learning can erase old-task closed-book performance within a few optimization steps. (b) A matched request-level example exposes two stages of forgetting. During addressing forgetting, the correct Skill name recovers execution that the raw request no longer reaches. Continued optimization can later damage execution under the correct skill address itself. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM) , which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory . The reactivation diagnostic exposes the Address–Execution split at individual-skill granularity; FSM operationalizes the same split more coarsely, using stage-level shards that each contain multiple Skills. At each stage, FSM trains and freezes one new LoRA executor while Address Memory learns request-to-shard associations without retaining historical requests or execution trajectories. The selected executor still identifies and composes the required Skills within its shard. At inference, Address Memory selects one shard from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a language-model generation. We make three contributions: • We construct a five-stage benchmark for continual skill internalization by partitioning 100 TaskBench Skills into disjoint Skill families and evaluating sequential acquisition, retention, and autonomous closed-book access. • We identify a hierarchical forgetting pattern under canonical-name reactivation: closed-book execution can collapse while execution under the correct skill address remains recoverable, before that recoverability also erodes. • We introduce FSM , which separates plastic Address Memory from frozen Execution Memory. Across two task orders, FSM reaches 65.95% mean performance and 93.38% shard-routing accuracy, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay. 2 Related Work Skill Internalization. Agent Skills are commonly represented as procedural artifacts that are retrieved and inserted into the model context at inference time ( Li and others, 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Recent work studies how to convert this guidance into persistent model behavior. SKILL0 and SkillC learn to execute Skills with progressively less dependence on explicit Skill context ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Another line of work parameterizes procedural knowledge directly: Skill-to-LoRA and ParametricSkills map Skills into adapter parameters, while LatentSkill and PEAM move textual or experiential Skill information into in-weight representations ( Zhang and Qi, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . LifeSkill further studies online lifelong adaptation from Skill-guided experience ( Mao et al., 2026 ) . Together, these methods show that procedural guidance can be transferred from context into model parameters, and several introduce mechanisms for accumulating such capabilities over time. Our focus is the failure structure that emerges when internalized Skills are learned sequentially without Skill identity at test time. We distinguish loss of request-side access from loss of execution itself, and use this Address–Execution hierarchy to determine what should remain plastic and what should be protected during continual internalization. Continual Learning. Continual learning studies how models acquire new tasks without overwriting earlier competence. Replay preserves old examples, regularization constrains parameter changes, and architectural methods isolate or expand parameters for new tasks ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Li and Hoiem, 2018 ; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017 ; Rebuffi et al., 2017b ; Rusu et al., 2016 ) . The last family is especially relevant when different tasks require distinct behaviors. Adapter-based continual learning allocates task-specific parameters ( Madotto et al., 2021 ) ; EPI combines private parameter-efficient modules with a non-parametric task identifier so that the appropriate module can be recovered without storing old training data ( Wang et al., 2023c ) ; and MoCL continually adds and composes modules to preserve knowledge while supporting transfer ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . FSM falls within this modular parameter-isolation line, with its decomposition motivated by the failure structure of continual Skill internalization. In continual Skill internalization, our reactivation experiments show that request-to-Skill access can fail while conditional execution remains intact. FSM therefore isolates the acquired procedural execution in frozen multi-Skill shards and treats access as the updated memory state. 3 Continual Skill Internalization Problem setting. We consider a sequence of stages t = 1 , … , T t=1,\ldots,T , where each stage introduces a previously unseen skill set 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and corresponding request–workflow supervision. The skill sets are pairwise disjoint, and after stage t t the desired competence includes all skills in 𝒮 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mathcal{S}_{t} . For a request x x , successful closed-book execution requires the model to produce the correct request-conditioned workflow using only the raw request. Training may use stage-local workflow supervision and, for skill-guided baselines, textual skill cards. Evaluation is autonomous and closed-book: the model receives only x x , not a stage label, skill name, or catalog. This setting tests acquisition of new skills and retention of earlier skills under autonomous inference. Benchmark. We instantiate this stream using the public Microsoft TaskBench benchmark ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , partitioning its 100 canonical skills into five disjoint semantic families (Table 3 ). We use each family as a unit of continual acquisition: a capability package containing several related procedures. The five packages contain 40, 11, 21, 9, and 19 canonical skills. Requests can require multi-node workflows composed from several skills in the same package. Each stage contains 1,000 training requests, for 5,000 in total, and the five held-out sets contain 2,186 requests. The complete skill inventory and output contract appear in Appendix A . Table 1: TaskBench benchmark statistics. Each stage uses 1,000 training requests. Task Semantic family # Skills Eval T1 Daily Life 40 864 T2 Language / Speech 11 408 T3 Retrieval / Understanding 21 332 T4 Vision / Document 9 299 T5 Generation / Editing 19 283 Total – 100 2,186 Metrics. Our primary metric is exact-match task success (EM) , which requires the complete prescribed workflow output to be correct; for TaskBench this is the benchmark’s canonical graph exact match, but we refer to it simply as EM in the main text. The T1–T5 columns and their task-macro average all report this same quantity. We use three secondary diagnostics to interpret failures: Tool-choice accuracy checks whether the ordered tool sequence is correct while ignoring request-specific values; Argument-value F1 compares predicted and target ( skill , argument , value ) (\text{skill},\text{argument},\text{value}) tuples; and BWT measures final old-task EM minus EM immediately after that task was learned, with zero indicating no forgetting; additional benchmark-specific metrics appear in the appendix. Direct continual optimization rapidly eliminates old-task closed-book performance. Before introducing any mechanism for preservation, we first measure how direct continual optimization behaves when training moves away from an acquired task. Immediately after learning the old task, EM is 77.45% for SFT, 84.31% for GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and 84.07% for the SKILL0 ( Lu et al., 2026 ) curriculum. After optimization switches to the next task, old-task EM falls to zero at observed steps 8, 6, and 10, respectively, and remains there over the rest of the measured interval (Figure 2 ). Across hundreds of held-out requests, none of the old-task outputs remain exactly correct. Under the standard closed-book criterion, all three procedures therefore exhibit catastrophic forgetting of the previously internalized skill. This endpoint shows that retention has failed without revealing which part of the acquired capability was lost. Section 4 tests this distinction directly. 4 When Forgotten Skills Come Back 4.1 Correct-Skill-Address Reactivation Section 3 showed that old-task closed-book performance can fall to zero after continual optimization moves to a new task. That endpoint does not reveal whether the old procedure has been erased or whether the model has lost access to behavior that is still present. We distinguish these cases with a controlled reactivation intervention. We take a post-forgetting checkpoint that scores zero on all 408 closed-book T2 requests and supply only the correct skill address , given by the benchmark’s exact procedure identifier or identifiers required by each request. On the same frozen model, full-task EM recovers from 0 to 69.85%. The address provides no argument values, workflow steps, or target serialization, so the model must still construct the request-conditioned workflow. Because it also reveals the gold node identity, we use the correct skill address as a diagnostic rather than a pure access probe. Additional controls are reported in Appendix B.1 . A frozen-base control further separates address recognition from learned execution. On 408 T2 requests, frozen Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) selects the correct skill on 92.65% of examples when given the correct skill address but obtains 0% full-task EM; by contrast, the post-forgetting checkpoint recovers 69.85% under the same address after request-only performance reaches zero. Recognizing the supplied address alone therefore cannot account for the recovered behavior. We use Address for access to the relevant procedural state and Execution for producing the request-conditioned workflow once that state is available. This reversal shows that substantial execution remains available once the correct procedure identity is supplied; we call this regime skill-addressing forgetting . 4.2 Execution under the correct skill address erodes later Figure 2: Hierarchical forgetting during continual skill internalization. Top: during the T2 → \rightarrow T3 transition, closed-book Task2 EM can collapse while Task2 remains recoverable when the correct skill address is supplied; with continued optimization, execution under the correct skill address can also erode. The frozen-executor diagnostic preserves the old task while learning Task3. Bottom: five-stage evaluation matrices for four continual-learning conditions. Off-diagonal cells report closed-book / + Correct Skill Address EM. Across both rows, pale green denotes retained performance, pale yellow denotes addressing forgetting, and pale purple denotes execution forgetting. Diagonal cells show task-acquisition EM. The FSM column is our method. To see what happens after this access failure, Figure 2 follows the first 20 optimizer steps of the T2 → \rightarrow T3 transition, evaluating each checkpoint closed-book and with the correct skill address. When closed-book T2 first reaches zero, full-task EM under the correct skill address is still 76.96% for SFT, 84.07% for GRPO, and 77.70% for SKILL0. Because the paired measurements come from the same checkpoint, this gap shows a loss of autonomous closed-book access relative to the target-identity-assisted condition while conditional execution remains available. Further T3 optimization then reduces performance under the correct skill address from 77.45% to 58.82% for SFT, from 84.56% to 57.60% for GRPO, and from 85.29% to zero for SKILL0. We call this later failure skill-execution forgetting : even the correct address can no longer recover the earlier behavior. The bottom matrices show the same ordering across other continual-learning methods: closed-book performance can collapse before execution under the correct skill address. This diagnostic operates at individual-skill granularity. FSM applies the same functional separation at shard granularity: routing selects a multi-skill capability package, while the selected executor still performs within-shard skill selection, composition, and execution. 5 Factorized Skill Memory Section 4 separates request-side access from execution at individual-skill granularity. FSM preserves this functional split without allocating one executor per skill: related skills are grouped into stage-level execution shards, and Address Memory learns only which shard to read. Formally, ℳ t = ( A t , ℰ t ) , \mathcal{M}_{t}=(A_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t}), where A t A_{t} is Address Memory and ℰ t = { E 1 , … , E t } \mathcal{E}_{t}=\{E_{1},\ldots,E_{t}\} is Execution Memory . Address remains plastic as new skill families arrive, whereas Execution Memory is append-only. At stage t t , FSM trains and freezes a fresh executor E t E_{t} on 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} ; current requests update Address with shard identity t t and are then discarded. Historical requests and workflow trajectories are never replayed. Each shard contains 9–40 canonical skills, so shard routing only narrows the execution space to a capability package. It does not replace within-shard skill selection: the chosen executor must still recover the required skill sequence, request-specific arguments, and dependencies from the raw request. At inference, Address selects one shard and only that executor performs language-model generation. Figure 3 summarizes the write-and-read process; Appendix A provides further details. Figure 3: Factorized Skill Memory (FSM). Left: memory write. At stage t t , current requests update Address Memory while a fresh executor E t = ℬ ⊕ Δ t E_{t}=\mathcal{B}\oplus\Delta_{t} is trained from the frozen base and a stage-specific LoRA. The completed executor is frozen and appended to Execution Memory as a new skill-family shard. Right: memory read. Address maps the raw request to p ⁡ ( j ∣ x ) p(j\mid x) , selects j ⋆ j^{\star} , and reads one frozen execution shard. Only E j ⋆ E_{j^{\star}} performs language-model generation. 5.1 Execution Memory: Immutable Parametric Shards Let B B denote the shared frozen base model. At stage t t , FSM initializes a fresh LoRA executor E t = B ⊕ Δ t E_{t}=B\oplus\Delta_{t} , trains Δ t \Delta_{t} only on current-stage skill-execution supervision, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to the bank, ℰ t = ℰ t − 1 ∪ { E t } \mathcal{E}_{t}=\mathcal{E}_{t-1}\cup\{E_{t}\} . No subsequent stage updates an earlier Δ j \Delta_{j} . This boundary follows the failure pattern in Section 4 : conditional execution can survive after request-side access has failed, so FSM protects the parameters that store execution and places subsequent adaptation in Address Memory. Low-rank adapters provide a compact implementation of these isolated parametric writes ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Rebuffi et al., 2017a ; Houlsby et al., 2019 ) . Each shard stores a family of related skills rather than a single procedure. For example, the T1 shard contains 40 canonical skills; selecting T1 only determines which execution memory to read, while the executor still chooses and composes the required skills and produces the complete request-conditioned graph. The shared 8.2B backbone is stored once. The test request contains no task label, correct skill address, or skill catalog, so shard identity must be recovered from request text alone. Our deployed Address maps request text into a fixed-dimensional hashing representation and updates an incremental Naive Bayes classifier using only the current request pool with label t t . After the update, those requests are discarded; the retained state consists only of class and feature statistics. Address Memory can therefore absorb new request-to-shard associations without retaining historical requests while the executor bank stays fixed. 5.3 Single-Shard Memory Read At inference, FSM performs a hard memory read: j ⋆ = arg ⁡ max j ​ p Address ​ ( j ∣ x ) , y = E j ⋆ ​ ( x ) . j^{\star}=\arg\max_{j}p_{\mathrm{Address}}(j\mid x),\qquad y=E_{j^{\star}}(x). The read is single-shard but multi-skill: Address selects one capability package, and the chosen executor can compose several canonical skills from that package while resolving request-specific arguments and graph dependencies. The language-model cost is one executor generation per request. As Execution Memory grows, storage therefore increases with the number of frozen shards, while the per-request language-model cost remains a single executor generation. 7 Conclusion Correct-skill-address reactivation reveals a hierarchical forgetting pattern: closed-book execution can collapse while execution under the correct skill address remains substantially recoverable, and continued optimization can later erase that recoverability as well. FSM follows this distinction by keeping Address Memory plastic and storing acquired procedures in frozen, multi-skill Execution Memory shards that remain unchanged during later stages. Across two five-stage task orders, FSM reaches 65.9593.38percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay. These results support a simple design principle for continual skill memory: preserve acquired procedural content while allowing access to adapt as the skill stream grows. They also separate two remaining sources of error: Address determines which execution shard is reached, whereas the selected shard determines how well the requested workflow is executed. This decomposition makes retention failures more interpretable and suggests where additional capacity or supervision is most useful. AI Use Statement.
